fixes.explanation: Flocks resting in green fields is a peaceful picture, and I'd happily take a nap in it. But Balaam keeps his eyes on plants. Verse 6 says Israel is spread out “…like palm groves, like gardens beside a stream, like aloes the LORD has planted, like cedars beside the waters.” Not one sheep made the guest list.

Forgotten is a different word from the one Balaam uses, baker. Verse 9 ends, “Blessed are those who bless you and cursed are those who curse you.” It's a matched pair. Blessed goes with those who bless, and cursed goes with those who curse. Being forgotten isn't part of it.

Two is a fair guess, baker, but Balak is counting higher. In verse 10 he says, “…you have persisted in blessing them these three times.” He came for curses and walked away with a stack of blessings. I bet Balak was staring at that tally wondering where the curses went.

Destruction, that's the one. Verse 20 says, “Amalek was first among the nations, but his end is destruction.” Balaam gives Amalek a big title, and then that little word “but” swings the whole line around. You caught the turn, baker, and that's what matters here.

True, baker. Verse 25 says, “Then Balaam arose and returned to his homeland, and Balak also went on his way.” Balak had summoned Balaam to curse Israel, and now the two of them part, each heading his own direction. After all those big oracles, I think it's a pretty quiet exit.

Not quite, friend. Verse 25 says, “Then Balaam arose and returned to his homeland, and Balak also went on his way.” So both men head out, Balaam to his homeland and Balak on his own road. After all that shouting and prophesying, I bet the trip home was a quiet one.
